say.text: A 47-year-old engineer has bulging, aching veins down the inner thigh and calf. Duplex shows reflux in the great saphenous vein from the saphenofemoral junction, and he is fit for anaesthesia.
Which treatment does current practice offer first?

choices.label: Trendelenburg operation with flush ligation and stripping of the vein
Endothermal ablation by radiofrequency or laser, under tumescent anaesthesia
Graduated compression stockings to control the symptoms, worn all day
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: the stem says current practice. Ask which option a registrar would offer first today, and which one is the old exam answer.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the Trendelenburg operation is the answer most exam keys have given for saphenofemoral incompetence.
Your stem asks what current practice offers first, so the older key is not the test here. Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the old key. Check what the exam expected and what practice now does; they differ here.

say.text: The Trendelenburg operation is flush ligation of the saphenous vein at the junction, with its tributaries tied, plus stripping to the knee.
PYQs have expected it as the answer. Current NICE practice puts endothermal ablation first, then foam, and open surgery only if both are unsuitable.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because stockings do ease the ache and swelling, so any symptomatic leg seems to need them.
Ask whether this patient could have the definitive treatment. Relief of symptoms is a different question. Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure stockings were the answer. Symptom relief is not the same as treating the reflux.

say.text: Yes. Endothermal ablation is the current first-line treatment for truncal reflux, when the patient is suitable.

choices.label: I know this, skip the worked plan

say.text: Here is a correct plan for the same patient. Duplex confirms the reflux and he is fit, so endothermal ablation is offered first, under tumescent local anaesthesia.
If ablation is unsuitable, ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy comes next. Open surgery is for when both are unsuitable.
A classmate plans the same fit patient in four steps. Exactly one step is wrong.

1) Duplex confirms great saphenous reflux. 2) Offer the Trendelenburg operation with stripping as first-line. 3) If that is unsuitable, offer foam sclerotherapy. 4) Open surgery only if both are unsuitable. Which step is the mistake?

choices.label: Step 3: foam offered if the first option is unsuitable
Step 4: open surgery kept for when both options fail
Step 2: the Trendelenburg operation named as the first-line treatment
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: check each step against current practice, not the exam key of the past. Which step fails that test?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because foam is often taught for spider veins, so a foam step for a trunk looks misplaced.
Foam is not limited to small veins. Ask which vein size foam suits best, then choose again.
Foam mixes the sclerosant with air and displaces blood, so it works better than liquid in larger veins.
Liquid suits telangiectasias and small residual veins. Foam is the second-line option for a trunk when ablation is unsuitable.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because open surgery is the classic treatment for saphenofemoral incompetence, so it seems to belong at the front.
In current practice open surgery sits last, for when both others are unsuitable. Step 4 is not the mistake. Look at which treatment the plan puts first, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure surgery belongs first. That is the older picture; check which option current practice places first.

say.text: Yes. The plan names the Trendelenburg operation as first-line. Current practice offers endothermal ablation first, and the operation is the classic exam answer.
You found the mistake: step 2 offers the operation as the first treatment.
Which reason makes that step wrong?

choices.label: Current practice puts ablation first; the operation is the old key
It skips compression, which should come first for a fit patient
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: the mistake is about which treatment comes first today. Pick the reason that is about that choice.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because compression eases the aching, so a missing compression step looks like the real gap.
Compression is for symptoms when intervention is unsuitable or declined, so it is not the first move here. Choose again.
The mistake is the choice of first treatment. Endothermal ablation is current first-line for truncal reflux.
Stockings relieve symptoms, and are used when intervention is unsuitable or declined, in pregnancy, and after treatment.
Yes. The mistake is the first-line choice itself. The operation is the classic exam answer, and practice has moved past it.
A clinic asks who should get graduated compression stockings as the treatment itself.
Which patient fits?

choices.label: A fit adult with great saphenous reflux confirmed on duplex
An adult with recurrent varicose veins and a suitable vein
A pregnant woman with symptomatic varicose veins in the legs
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: for each patient, ask whether intervention is suitable and declined, or not an option at all.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because stockings do relieve symptoms, so a symptomatic patient seems covered by them.
Ask whether this patient is a candidate for the definitive treatment, and whether anything stops it. Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure stockings suit a symptomatic patient. They suit a patient who cannot or will not have intervention.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because recurrence sounds like a reason for more conservative care, so stockings look like the next step.
Recurrence does not change the rule. Check whether a suitable vein remains for treatment, then choose again.
Graduated stockings relieve symptoms. They are used when intervention is unsuitable or declined, in pregnancy, and after treatment.
NICE advises against offering hosiery as the treatment when interventional treatment is suitable.
Yes. Stockings relieve symptoms in pregnancy, one of the settings where they are the right choice.
Sclerotherapy injects a sclerosant that damages the lining of the vein, so the vein fibroses and closes.
The sclerosant is given as a liquid, or as a foam made by mixing it with air (the Tessari technique).
A woman has a cluster of thigh telangiectasias and reticular veins. Her saphenous veins are not refluxing.
Which sclerotherapy form suits these veins?

choices.label: Liquid sclerotherapy, injected directly into the small veins
Foam sclerotherapy, which displaces blood in the vein
Foam sclerotherapy, given in a larger volume for effect
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: the form should follow the size of the vein, and these are the smallest veins in the stem.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because foam is the more effective form, so the stronger-looking option feels safer.
Effectiveness depends on the size of the vein. Ask which vein size this stem describes, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure foam was the stronger form. Its advantage is in larger veins, not in small ones.

say.text: Foam displaces blood in a large lumen, so it is more effective than liquid in larger veins.
Liquid is best for telangiectasias, reticular veins and small residual varicosities.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because a bigger dose sounds like more treatment for the same veins.
The problem is the form, not the amount. Ask which form suits small veins, then choose again.
Yes. Liquid sclerotherapy is best for telangiectasias, reticular veins and small residual varicosities.
A classmate writes: 'The exam key names STS, so polidocanol is not a sclerosant.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: STS is the key, so polidocanol is not an accepted agent
Polidocanol has replaced STS, so the old key is wrong
STS is the classic key; polidocanol is also an accepted agent
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Hint: the question is whether the key makes the other agent wrong. What can a key that names one answer actually tell you?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the key names one agent, and a single named answer makes the other look wrong.
Check whether the key says the other agent is wrong, or only names a classic answer. Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure the key rules the other agent out. A key names the classic answer; it does not rule out an accepted one.

say.text: Sodium tetradecyl sulphate is the classic answer in the exam key, and polidocanol is also a common sclerosant.
Polidocanol is an equally accepted modern agent, so the key names one answer without making the other wrong.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because a newer name feels as if it should replace the old one, so the key looks out of date.
Newer does not mean the classic answer is wrong. Ask whether both agents can be accepted, then choose again.
Yes. STS is the classic key answer, and polidocanol is an equally accepted modern agent.
